items.title: The most important open problem in mathematics
items.claim: Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all non-trivial zeros of the zeta function lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. The conjecture controls the distribution of primes among integers. Proving (or disproving) it has been unsolved for 165 years.
items.prompt: Why do we care about complex zeros of a strange function?

options.text: The distribution of prime numbers is encoded in the zeros of the Riemann zeta function — proving the Riemann hypothesis would establish a vast number of theorems in number theory that are currently conditional on it
It tells us the value of zeta at integer points
It's part of the definition of pi

items.reveal:
Riemann's only paper on number theory (1859) defined the analytic continuation of the zeta function and noted that the function has 'trivial zeros' at -2, -4, -6, ... and other 'non-trivial zeros' in the strip 0 less than Re(s) less than 1. He conjectured all non-trivial zeros lie exactly on Re(s) = 1/2.

The Prime Number Theorem (Hadamard, de la Vallée Poussin, 1896) says the count of primes up to x is asymptotically x / ln x. The Riemann hypothesis would tighten the error term enormously.

Thousands of theorems in modern number theory are stated 'assuming RH'. A proof would make them unconditional. Conversely, a disproof would force major rewrites.

The first 10 trillion non-trivial zeros have all been computed and verified to lie on Re(s) = 1/2 (Gourdon, 2004). This doesn't prove the hypothesis.

The Clay Mathematics Institute lists it as one of seven Millennium Prize Problems, with a $1,000,000 reward. So far, only Poincaré (Perelman, 2003) has been solved.
items.why: Primes look like a chaotic distribution. The Riemann hypothesis says they have hidden, beautiful regularity controlled by complex analysis — and 165 years of effort haven't proved or disproved it.

items.title: Matrices don't commute — and that's why quantum mechanics works
items.claim: AB is not generally equal to BA for matrices. The order of operations matters. This isn't a defect — it's the most important feature of matrix algebra and the mathematical foundation of quantum uncertainty.

options.text: Matrices represent linear transformations of vectors; applying transformation A then B is generally not the same as B then A. The non-commutativity reflects that composition of transformations in higher dimensions does NOT commute in general
AB = BA always works for invertible matrices

items.reveal:
For matrices, AB and BA are generally different — and AB is well-defined only when A's columns equal B's rows. Even for square matrices of the same size, AB and BA can differ wildly.

Example: A = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], B = [[1, 0], [1, 1]].
AB = [[2, 1], [1, 1]].
BA = [[1, 1], [1, 2]]. Different.

When does AB = BA? Some special cases: scalar multiples of identity; same diagonal matrix; simultaneously diagonalisable matrices; powers of the same matrix.

The commutator [A, B] = AB - BA measures the non-commutativity. For ordinary numbers it's always zero; for matrices it can be anything.

In QUANTUM MECHANICS:
- Physical observables are represented as matrices (or operators on Hilbert space).
- The commutator of position and momentum: [x, p] = i * hbar. Non-zero!
- Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: the variance of two non-commuting observables, in any state, has a lower bound proportional to the commutator. You can't simultaneously know position and momentum precisely.

This is not a measurement limitation — it's a structural feature of the math. Eigenvectors of non-commuting matrices are different; states have to choose between definite x and definite p.

Lie groups and algebras: continuous symmetry transformations form groups whose generators are matrices with commutation relations. The group SU(3) underlies the strong nuclear force; SU(2) describes weak force and quantum spin; U(1) describes electromagnetism. The standard model of particle physics is built from non-commuting matrices.

In computer graphics: rotation matrices in 3D don't commute (mentioned in another card). The order matters when composing transformations.
items.why: Multiplication seems naturally commutative. For matrices it isn't — and the depth of this fact is that quantum mechanics, particle physics, computer graphics, and most of modern physics rely on it.

items.title: Integration by parts is the product rule played backwards
items.claim: The product rule: d(uv)/dx = u'v + uv'. Rearrange: uv' = d(uv)/dx - u'v. Integrate: integral of uv' dx = uv - integral of u'v dx. The formula isn't a separate tool — it's the product rule, integrated.

options.text: Choose u as the type higher in 'ILATE' priority: Inverse trig, Logarithmic, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential. These tend to become simpler when differentiated; choosing them as u makes u'v easier to integrate than the original

items.reveal_title: Integration by parts and clever choices
items.reveal:
Integration by parts: integral of u dv = uv - integral of v du.

The formula always works mathematically, but the resulting integral can be HARDER than the original if you choose u and dv poorly. The ILATE heuristic helps:
- I: Inverse trig (arctan, arcsin)
- L: Logarithmic (ln x)
- A: Algebraic (polynomials)
- T: Trigonometric (sin, cos)
- E: Exponential (e^x)

Choose u as the FIRST function appearing in this list. Choose dv as the LAST.

Why: logarithmic and inverse trig functions become algebraic when differentiated; polynomials become lower-degree polynomials. Exponentials and most trig functions stay similar under differentiation, so we'd rather integrate them.

Classical applications:
- integral of x e^x dx: u = x, dv = e^x dx. Result: x e^x - e^x + C.
- integral of x sin x dx: u = x, dv = sin x dx. Result: -x cos x + sin x + C.
- integral of ln x dx: u = ln x, dv = dx. Result: x ln x - x + C.
- integral of x^2 e^x dx: apply twice.

Tabular integration (D-I tabular method) systematises repeated applications.

The Frullani integral, Bessel functions, and many special-function identities come from clever integration by parts. It's not just a textbook drill; it's the algebraic shadow of one of the deepest theorems in calculus (the fundamental theorem applied to product structures).
items.why: Integration by parts is taught as a mechanical technique. It's the product rule running backwards — and the ILATE heuristic is empirical wisdom about which functions are easier to differentiate than integrate.
